01.note: A document carried the signatures of two witnesses, Rava and Rav Aha bar Adda. Its holder brought it before Rava, who said: this is my signature, but I never signed anything together with Rav Aha bar Adda. Rava bound the man and he admitted the forgery. Rava then asked how he had copied Rav Aha bar Adda's signature, since that Sage's hands shake. The man said he had rested his hands on the rope of a narrow footbridge; some say he stood on a wobbly water skin as he wrote.
01.why: The Gemara has been discussing forged documents: Abaye's warning about where numbers fall on a line, and two altered bills of sale that Abaye exposed. This third case is caught by one of the supposed signers himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose real signature appears on the forged document; he exposes the forger.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Adda
people.about: A Sage whose hands shake, so his signature is distinctive; his signature was forged.

terms.meaning: Subjected to physical coercion, used here by the judge to force the holder of a suspect document to confess.

02.note: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba had signed as a witness on a receipt showing that a woman had been paid her marriage contract. A woman whose name was on the receipt told him: it was not I. He answered her: but it was you. Abaye said that although a Torah scholar does not usually look closely at women to identify them, once he does say he is sure, his identification holds.
02.why: Just before, the Gemara told a version in which Rav Yirmeya doubted the woman's identity and Abaye let him retract his signature. This version has him identifying her firmly, and Abaye explains why that changes things.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who signed as a witness on the woman's receipt.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who comments on how far a scholar's identification of a woman can be trusted.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife at marriage, promising her a sum of money if he divorces her or dies.
A signed document showing a woman has already collected her marriage contract, so she cannot collect it again.

03.note: A band of Arabs came to Pumbedita and seized people's land. Landowners asked Abaye to write a second deed for each property, so that if one were taken they would still hold the other. Abaye said he could not, since Rav Safra rules that two deeds are not written for one field. They kept badgering him, so he told his scribe to write the deeds over erased writing, with the witnesses signing on unerased paper, which makes a document invalid. Rav Aha bar Minyumi objected that if the erased writing were still legible the deed would be valid. Abaye answered that he had meant the scribe to write and erase only letters of the alphabet, not a real document.
03.why: The Gemara has just cited a baraita that a document erased or smudged is valid if its writing can still be made out. Rav Aha bar Minyumi applies that very ruling to Abaye's trick.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage the landowners ask for duplicate deeds.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage whose ruling against writing two deeds for one field Abaye cites.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Minyumi
people.about: A Sage who challenges Abaye's instructions to the scribe.

terms.meaning: A document proving ownership of land.

When land is taken from a buyer by the seller's creditor or a rightful owner, the buyer can collect his loss from the seller's other sold land by showing his deed. Two deeds could let him collect twice.

04.note: A woman gave a man money to buy land for her as her agent. He bought the land without a guarantee. She came before Rav Nahman, who told the agent that she could say: I sent you to help me, not to harm me, so the purchase made on her behalf was void. Rav Nahman told the agent to buy the land from the seller himself without a guarantee, and then sell it to her with one.
04.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a bill of sale that leaves out the guarantee still carries one. This case of an agent who bought without a guarantee is set beside that debate.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage the woman brings her complaint to.

terms.meaning: A seller's promise to repay the buyer if the land is later taken away by the seller's creditor or by someone who proves it belongs to him.
Someone appointed to act for another; what he does on the appointer's behalf counts as if the appointer did it.

05.note: Rabbi Abba owed money to Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, and the case came before Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha. Rabbi Abba said he had repaid the debt in front of two named people. The judge said those two must come and testify. Rabbi Abba protested that a borrower need not repay in front of witnesses. The judge answered that he was following Rabbi Abba's own teaching, in Rav's name: whoever says he repaid in front of named people must bring them. Rabbi Abba cited a ruling that follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the judge replied that he only meant Rabbi Abba should bring them if he could.
05.why: The Gemara has just suggested that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree about whether a litigant must back up a claim he did not need to make. This case is its example of that kind of verifying.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: The lender, owed money by Rabbi Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The borrower, who says he already repaid.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: The judge who hears the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.

06.note: A judge let a creditor take over a debtor's property to collect his debt before the creditor had made any claim against the debtor himself. Rav Hanin, son of Rav Yeiva, overruled the judge and expelled the creditor. Rava said: who is wise enough to rule this way, if not Rav Hanin? Rava explained that a person's property acts as his guarantor, and a creditor may not collect from a guarantor before first claiming from the debtor.
06.why: The Gemara has been discussing guarantors and when a creditor may turn to them. Rava stretches the rule that a guarantor is not approached first to cover the debtor's own property.

people.name: Rav Hanin, son of Rav Yeiva
people.about: A Sage who overrules the judge and removes the creditor from the property.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who praises Rav Hanin's ruling and explains it.

terms.meaning: A person who promises to pay a loan if the borrower does not.
The early collection of the Sages' rulings that the Gemara discusses.

07.note: A man had guaranteed a loan. The borrower died, leaving orphans who were minors, and the guarantor repaid the creditor before telling them. He then wanted the orphans to repay him. Rav Pappa said repaying a creditor is a mitzva, and minor orphans are not obligated in mitzvot. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said perhaps the father had handed the creditor bundles of money before he died. The Gemara asks where the two reasons differ, and answers: when the father admitted before dying that he had not paid, or when he died while excommunicated over the debt.
07.why: The case before it involved a creditor who collected before claiming from the debtor. Here a guarantor paid first, and the Gemara goes on to a ruling sent from the Land of Israel that follows Rav Huna in the excommunication case.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who exempts minor orphans because they are not obligated in mitzvot.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who exempts them because their father may already have paid.

terms.meaning: A commandment; a religious duty.
Money the dead man may have handed the creditor before his death, which his young children would not know about.
Placed under a ban by the court; here, for refusing to cooperate in repaying a debt.

08.note: Moshe bar Atzari had guaranteed the marriage contract of his daughter-in-law. His son, Rav Huna, was a young Torah scholar who was short of money. Abaye asked: is there no one to advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife, so she can collect her marriage contract from his father, and then remarry her? Rava objected that the mishna requires such a husband to vow to take no benefit from her. Abaye replied that not everyone who divorces does so in court. In the end it came out that Rav Huna was a priest, who may not marry a divorcee. Abaye said: as people say, poverty follows the poor.
08.why: The mishna quotes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a husband whose wife's marriage contract has a guarantor must vow off her when he divorces her, to block exactly this ploy. Afterward the Gemara asks how Abaye could suggest it when he condemned such advice elsewhere.

people.name: Moshe bar Atzari
people.about: Guarantor of his daughter-in-law's marriage contract; Rav Huna's father.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Moshe bar Atzari's son, a young Torah scholar short of money, who turns out to be a priest.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who proposes the divorce-and-remarry plan.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects to Abaye's plan.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife at marriage, promising her a sum of money if he divorces her or dies.
Someone who promises to pay if the person primarily responsible does not.
The early collection of the Sages' rulings that the Gemara discusses.

09.note: Students asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz about the verse on a woman who gives birth to a girl. Its letters, written without vowels, could be read as seventy days of impurity instead of two weeks. He answered with an argument: the Torah doubles the period of purity after a girl compared with a boy, so it must also double the impurity, from seven days to two weeks. After they left he went after them and said: you do not need that proof. We read it as two weeks, and the way the text is read is what counts.
09.why: Rabbi Yohanan has listed Sages who hold that the Torah's traditional reading, not its bare written letters, decides the law. This baraita is the Gemara's proof for Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz
people.about: A Sage whose students question him about a verse in Leviticus.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
In a state of ritual impurity, which bars a person from the Temple and from holy things for a set time.
The traditional pronunciation of the Torah's words, which the written text, having no vowels, does not show.

10.note: When Rabba bar Hana went down to Babylonia, his uncle Rabbi Hiyya asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: my brother's son is going down to Babylonia; may he teach? May he judge? May he declare firstborn animals permitted? To each the answer was yes. When Rav went down to Babylonia, Rabbi Hiyya asked the same about his sister's son. Rav was allowed to teach and to judge, but not to declare firstborn animals permitted.
10.why: The Gemara has been asking whether permission to judge given in the Land of Israel works in Babylonia, and now asks what that permission consists of. It goes on to ask why Rav was called a sister's son and refused one part.

people.name: Rabba bar Hana
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's brother's son, setting out for Babylonia.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Uncle of Rabba bar Hana and of Rav, who asks permission on their behalf.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the one who grants permission to teach and judge.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, called his sister's son, also setting out for Babylonia.

terms.meaning: The male firstborn of a kosher animal belongs to the Temple and may not be eaten, but if it gets a permanent blemish it may be eaten. A Sage had to judge the blemish.
To judge money cases; with permission, a judge who erred was exempt from paying for his mistake.

11.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to a place where people were kneading dough while ritually impure, sure it would stay pure. They told him a visiting Torah scholar had taught that swamp water does not make food able to become impure, so they used it. He had actually taught that "water of eggs", egg white, does not, and they had misheard. They had also misunderstood a teaching that the swamp water of two rivers is unfit for the purification water of the red heifer, taking it to mean that this water did not count as water at all. At that time, the Sages decreed that a student may not teach unless his teacher gives him permission.
11.why: The Gemara asked why a scholar who knows the law would need permission merely to teach what is permitted and forbidden. This incident is its answer: a careless teacher can mislead a whole town.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; he discovers the town's mistake.

terms.meaning: Food can become ritually impure only after it has been wetted by water or certain other liquids.
Water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer to purify people from contact with the dead; it must be running water.

12.note: Rabbi Hiyya saw a man standing in a cemetery and asked him: are you not the son of a certain priest? Priests may not have contact with the dead. The man said yes, but explained that his father had been a man with "raised eyes" who set his eyes on a divorcee and married her, and so disqualified his son from the priesthood.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage surprised to see a priest's son in a cemetery.

terms.meaning: A man who wanted whatever he saw, even what was forbidden to him.
A priest is forbidden to marry a divorced woman; a son of such a marriage loses the status and duties of a priest.

13.note: The house of the Nasi appointed a judge who was not learned. The judge told Yehuda bar Nahmani, Reish Lakish's interpreter, to stand over him as interpreter while he lectured. Yehuda bar Nahmani bent over to listen, but the judge said nothing at all. So the interpreter began on his own with Habakkuk's verse: Woe to him who says to the wood, awake, to the dumb stone, arise; it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath in it. He added that God will one day punish those who appoint such judges.
13.why: The Gemara has been teaching that a judge must be independent and not seek gifts. Afterward Reish Lakish compares appointing an unfit judge to planting an idolatrous tree, and Rav Ashi reads "gods of silver and gold" as judges appointed for money.

people.name: Yehuda bar Nahmani
people.about: Reish Lakish's interpreter, told to serve the unlearned judge.

terms.meaning: The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.
A man who stood beside a Sage during a public lecture and repeated and explained his words aloud to the audience.

14.note: Rav's host, with whom he sometimes stayed, came before him for a judgment. Rav asked: are you not my host? He said yes, and that he had a case to be judged. Rav told him he was disqualified from judging him, and told Rav Kahana to go out and judge it. Rav Kahana saw that the host was acting haughtily, and told him: if you will listen, listen; if not, I will take Rav out of your ears.
14.why: The Gemara is reading the verse "You shall not respect persons in judgment," which Rabbi Yehuda takes to mean a judge must not recognize a litigant as a friend. Rav's refusal to judge his own host puts that into practice.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who refuses to judge the case of a man who hosted him.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage Rav sends to judge the case instead.

terms.term: take Rav out of your ears
terms.meaning: Rav Kahana's warning that the host's tie to Rav would not help him in court.

15.note: Rabban Gamliel asked for seven Sages to come early to the upper room to intercalate the year, and in the morning he found eight. He said: whoever came up without permission must go down. Shmuel HaKatan stood and said it was he, and that he had come only to learn the practical law, not to take part. Rabban Gamliel told him: sit, my son, sit; every year would be fit to be intercalated by you, but the Sages said only those invited may do it. The Gemara adds that it was not really Shmuel HaKatan who had come uninvited but someone else; he spoke up to spare that person shame.
15.why: A baraita rules that the year may be intercalated only by those the Nasi invited, and this incident shows that rule in force. The Gemara then traces the habit of taking blame to spare another's shame back through Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, who summons seven Sages to intercalate the year.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: A Sage who claims to be the uninvited eighth.

terms.meaning: To add an extra month to the year so that the lunar calendar stays in step with the seasons and Passover falls in spring. Only a court of Sages could decide it.
The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.

16.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was teaching when he smelled garlic, and said: whoever ate garlic should leave. Rabbi Hiyya stood up and left, and then everyone stood up and left. The next morning Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son, found Rabbi Hiyya and asked: are you the one who upset my father? Rabbi Hiyya answered: such a thing should not happen among the Jewish people. He had not eaten garlic; he left so that whoever had would not be shamed.
16.why: The Gemara tells this as a parallel to Shmuel HaKatan claiming to be the uninvited Sage, and then asks where Rabbi Hiyya learned this conduct.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the teacher who cannot bear the smell of garlic.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who walks out of the lecture.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who questions Rabbi Hiyya the next day.

17.note: A woman came to Rabbi Meir's study hall and said: Rabbi, one of you betrothed me through intercourse. Rabbi Meir got up, wrote her a bill of divorce and gave it to her. Then all the others got up, wrote bills of divorce and gave them to her, so the man was never singled out.
17.why: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Hiyya learned to take blame on himself to spare another's shame. This is its answer, and the chain then runs back to Shmuel HaKatan and Shecaniah ben Jehiel.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Head of the study hall, who writes the woman a bill of divorce first.

terms.meaning: One of the ways a man could make a woman legally his betrothed; she could not marry anyone else until he divorced her.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage or betrothal.

18.note: After the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the Divine Spirit left the Jewish people, but they still made use of a Divine Voice. Once the Sages were reclining in the upper room of the house of Gurya in Jericho, and a Divine Voice told them: there is one here fit for the Divine Presence to rest on him as on Moses, but his generation is not worthy. The Sages looked to Hillel the Elder. When he died they said of him: alas, the pious man, alas, the humble man, a disciple of Ezra.
18.why: The Gemara has just praised Shmuel HaKatan's piety; this story about Hillel opens a teaching of the Sages whose next part tells the same of Shmuel HaKatan.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: The Sage the others take to be the one the Divine Voice meant.

terms.meaning: The spirit of prophecy, which the text says left the Jewish people after the last prophets.
A voice from Heaven, described here as what the Sages still heard after prophecy ended.
God's presence resting on a person, as it rested on Moses in prophecy.

19.note: Another time the Sages were reclining in an upper room in Yavne, and a Divine Voice said: there is one here fit for the Divine Presence, but his generation is not worthy. The Sages looked to Shmuel HaKatan. When he died they said of him: alas, the pious man, alas, the humble man, a disciple of Hillel. As he was dying he said: Shimon and Yishmael to the sword, their companions to execution, the rest of the people to plunder, and great troubles will come upon the world. The Sages wanted to say the same of Yehuda ben Bava, but the hour was torn, for those executed by the government are not eulogized.
19.why: It completes a teaching that set Shmuel HaKatan beside Hillel the Elder, told because the Gemara had just praised Shmuel HaKatan for taking blame to spare another's shame.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage the others take to be the one the Divine Voice meant; a disciple of Hillel.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: Named in Shmuel HaKatan's dying words as one who will die by the sword; the Nasi of the Great Sanhedrin.

people.name: Yishmael
people.about: Named with Shimon in Shmuel HaKatan's dying words; the High Priest.

people.name: Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage executed by the government, so the Sages could not eulogize him.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven, described here as what the Sages still heard after prophecy ended.
God's presence resting on a person, as it rested on Moses in prophecy.
The moment was lost: the Sages could not give him the eulogy they wanted.

20.note: Rabban Gamliel went to ask permission from a governor in Syria and was delayed in coming back. The Sages intercalated the year on condition that Rabban Gamliel would want it. When he returned and said, I want it, the year was found to be intercalated.
20.why: A baraita rules that the year may be intercalated only if the Nasi wants it. This incident shows how the court kept that rule while he was away, by making the extra month depend on his consent.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, away in Syria when the year needed to be intercalated.

terms.meaning: To add an extra month to the year so that the lunar calendar stays in step with the seasons and Passover falls in spring. Only a court of Sages could decide it.
The president of the Great Sanhedrin, the head of the Sages' court and of the Jewish community.
